title: How to Sit With Feedback You Don't Agree With
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni of Empathy Elevated offers a practical method for handling feedback that feels unfair, using a software engineer facing vague code-review criticism as the example. She warns that high performers are quick to build counterarguments and that unfair feedback may still be true. A pulse check separates accuracy from emotion and intent by asking whether the feedback is true, whether it feels unfair and what the person is actually trying to say. She suggests treating disagreeable feedback like a suspect bug report to reproduce, setting a time box for deciding, and optionally asking an AI tool for three interpretations to avoid assuming bad intent. The final decision is to adopt, adapt or respectfully decline. She urges closing the thread on purpose, because unresolved feedback compounds and drains attention from real work.
points: Feeling that feedback is unfair is not the same as the feedback being untrue, so accuracy should be assessed separately from emotion.
Both dismissing the feedback outright and ruminating on it are failure modes that cost either the signal or hours of attention.
Treating disagreeable feedback like a suspect bug report encourages reproducing the conditions under which it is true.
A time box and a request for clarification keep vague feedback from becoming endless replaying.
The process ends by deciding to adopt, adapt or decline and then closing the loop, because unresolved feedback quietly compounds.
quotes: Sure, it might really be unfair. Criticism of something largely out of your control, or not meeting criteria that were never explicitly set. Remember, though: what isn’t fair may or may not be true.
There are two failure modes from here. Absolute dismissal costs you the signal. Rumination costs you hours of attention you did not budget for.
Treat feedback you disagree with like a suspect bug report. Do not shut the door on it immediately.
Set a time box. This takes self-control, but saves you time in waffling on the actions to take and the thoughts replaying.
You can paste the feedback directly into your favorite AI LLM and ask: What are three interpretations of this, so I don’t assume bad intent?
You are not outsourcing your judgment. You own your human judgment. But you are giving yourself another angle to consider.
As for your go-forward decision at the end of the time window and when more clarity is reached, it is your decision: adopt, adapt, or respectfully decline.
The worst outcome isn’t unfair feedback itself; it’s when it never gets resolved in your own mind.
